questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining search space, so the number of steps is log n. It requires the array to be sorted first, which is the prerequisite that makes the speed-up possible.

questions.prompt: Binary search requires the input array to be:

options.text: A power of two in length

questions.explanation: The algorithm decides which half to discard by comparing the target to the middle element, which is only meaningful if the array is ordered. On unsorted data a linear scan is the fallback.

questions.prompt: In binary search, the midpoint is often computed as low + (high - low) / 2 rather than (low + high) / 2. Why?

options.text: To avoid integer overflow when low and high are large

questions.explanation: For large indices, low + high can exceed the integer range and wrap around to a negative value. The subtraction form computes the same midpoint without ever forming the oversized sum.

questions.prompt: The two-pointer technique on a sorted array to find a pair with a given sum runs in:
questions.explanation: One pointer starts at each end and they move inward based on whether the current sum is too big or too small. Each pointer traverses the array at most once, giving linear time.

questions.prompt: To remove duplicates in place from a sorted array, the two-pointer approach uses:

options.text: A slow pointer marking the write position and a fast pointer scanning ahead
A hash set of seen values

questions.explanation: The fast pointer scans; whenever it finds a value different from the last kept one, the slow pointer advances and stores it. This compacts unique values in O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time to search for an element in an unsorted array?
questions.explanation: Linear search must inspect each element and the target may be last or absent. Without order there is no way to rule out large parts of the array, so binary search cannot be used.

questions.prompt: Binary search can be adapted to find the first position where a monotonic predicate becomes true. This general pattern is often called:
questions.explanation: When a condition is false then true across a range, binary search locates the boundary in O(log range). This turns many optimisation problems into a search over candidate answers.

questions.prompt: The fast-and-slow pointer variant of two pointers is typically used to:

options.text: Detect a cycle or find the middle of a sequence

questions.explanation: One pointer moving twice as fast as the other meets it inside a cycle, and sits at the midpoint when the fast one reaches the end. This is Floyd's technique applied to arrays or lists.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does binary search make in the worst case on an array of 1000 elements?
questions.explanation: The worst case is ceil(log2 1000), which is 10. Linear search on the same array would average about 500 comparisons.

questions.prompt: When is a simple linear search preferable to binary search?

options.text: When many searches will be run on static data
When the array is very large and sorted
When the data is unsorted and will be searched only once
When the array is stored on disk

questions.explanation: Sorting to enable binary search costs O(n log n), which is not worth it for a single lookup on unsorted data. Repeated searches on static data, by contrast, amortise that sorting cost.
